newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: N.Korean defector arrives in Philippines-military.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean defector arrives in Philippines-military.

text.p: North Korean defector Hwang Jang-yop flew into the Philippines under a veil of secrecy on Tuesday and was immediately taken by helicopter to a haven in a northern mountain resort city, military officers said.

They said Hwang was accompanied by three other passengers, including at least one South Korean diplomat, when he arrived at the Clark airbase north of Manila on a chartered Air China commercial plane from the southeastern Chinese city of Xiamen.
A defence ministry officer said the helicopters were headed to Baguio, about 200 km (125 miles) north of Manila.
The Clark military officer, who said he was present when Hwang arrived, said the Koreans stayed at the Clark terminal building for 30 minutes before the helicopters took him and his party away.
President Fidel Ramos said in Manila he had no information on the matter but was asking the Department of Foreign Affairs to verify the report.

"No, I have not received a report to that effect," Ramos told an impromptu news conference. "In any case, I will verify that and later on whatever be the result, we will have the Department of Foreign Affairs issue a statement."
It was not immediately clear why Baguio was chosen to shelter Hwang but a presidential summer mansion secluded from the public is located in the resort city.
A military source said he was also verifying a report that a Korean facility was situated in Baguio.
Hwang, North Korea's top ideologue and most senior official to defect from the Stalinist homeland, sought shelter at the South Korean consulate in Beijing on February 12.

On Monday, a senior South Korean official said Hwang would stay in a third country "for a considerable period of time" before coming to South Korea. There were earlier reports he might stay in the third country for as long as a month.

Hwang's defection had muddied ties between China and the two Koreas, bitter rivals since the 1950-1953 Korean War, and forced Beijing to choose between a new capitalist friend in the South and an old communist ally in the North.
